opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in a couple of layers. First and foremost, our job is to make the underlying models really good at agentic work: following long multi-step instructions, using tools reliably, recovering when something goes wrong, and knowing when to stop and ask instead of barreling ahead. A lot of what makes an agent work or fail comes down to the model's judgment in those moments, and that's something we can improve directly in training.

On top of that, we want to show people what's possible. Things like Claude Code or the agent SDK aren't meant to be the only way to build agents. They're a reference point that says, "here's a pattern that works, here's how we think about tool design and context management." And honestly, building those things ourselves teaches us a ton. When we dogfood an agent internally, we find the rough edges in the model fast, and that feeds straight back into the next round of training.

One thing I push on a lot is that people overcomplicate their agent architectures. Often the best system is surprisingly simple: a good model, a well-designed set of tools, and a loop. Most of the effort should go into the tools themselves. Make them clear, give them good descriptions, make the errors informative, almost like you're writing documentation for a new engineer on your team. We've seen that matter more than elaborate orchestration frameworks.

So I'd say our role is partly building capability, partly setting good patterns, and partly doing it safely. As agents get more autonomy, the questions about oversight, permissions, and making sure a human can stay in the loop on consequential actions become really central. We want to be the ones figuring that out early rather than bolting it on later.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot. The way I'd frame it is that Anthropic's job is less to build the one true agent and more to make the model itself a really good agent, and then make it as easy as possible for other people to build on top of that.

When we first started with Claude Code, it was honestly kind of a surprise how well it worked. We built it as an internal tool, a pretty thin harness around the model, and the thing that made it good wasn't the scaffolding, it was that the model was actually capable of doing long, multi-step tasks on its own. And I think that's the lesson: historically a lot of agent work was about compensating for model weaknesses. You'd build these elaborate chains and routers and retry loops because the model couldn't be trusted to just do the thing. Every generation of models, a lot of that scaffolding just gets deleted. So part of our role is to keep pushing the model in that direction, so that the agent logic lives inside the model rather than around it. Things like tool use, being able to work for hours without drifting, knowing when to check in with the user versus just proceeding, those are model properties, and we train for them directly.

The second piece is building a few first-party products ourselves, like Claude Code, because you learn a huge amount by being your own customer. We find the rough edges before anyone else does, and that feeds straight back into training. But we try to be pretty deliberate about not boiling the ocean there. The surface area of what people want agents to do is enormous, and we're not going to build all of it.

So the third piece is the ecosystem. The SDK, the tool-use APIs, things like MCP, those exist so that people can take the same harness we use internally and point it at their own problems. I'd much rather have a thousand teams building agents on Claude that we never would have thought of than try to own the whole stack. Our comparative advantage is the model and the safety work around it. Making sure an agent that has real permissions on your machine behaves predictably is a hard problem, and that's something we care about getting right at the model level, because it's not something you can fully bolt on afterward.

astra-6.text:
I think our role is both to make the models more capable and to make it easier for people to build reliable systems around them. A model being good at answering a question is different from being able to work through a task, use tools, notice when something went wrong, and recover.

There’s also a lot we learn by building with the models ourselves. You run into limitations that aren’t obvious in a single-turn conversation, and that helps inform what to improve in the next model.

But I don’t think that means we need to build every agent application. We want developers to have strong building blocks and room to experiment. Often, the right starting point is a simple workflow, and you add autonomy where it actually helps.

sol-6.1.text:
I think our role is to make the models really good at the building blocks of being an agent: using tools, following instructions, and working through longer tasks reliably. And then to learn from people building on top of them—where does the model get stuck, where does it need more context, where does it need to ask a question?

There’s a lot around the model that matters, too: how you manage context, how you give it feedback, and how you decide what it can do autonomously. I don’t think there’s one architecture that’s right for every application. We want to provide strong models and useful primitives so developers can experiment and build the systems that make sense for their users.
